title: IB Design Technology Exam Technique for November
summary: IB Design Technology exam technique for November: understand each paper, manage your time and write precise answers that match the marks available.
body_markdown:
November exams have a peculiar feeling. While much of the school year seems to be beginning, yours is narrowing toward a few decisive hours.


The best **IB Design Technology exam technique** is not to write everything you know. It is to identify what the command term requires, use subject-specific knowledge, apply it to the context and stop when you have earned the available marks. For November candidates, the final three weeks should therefore move from diagnosis to deliberate practice, then to full timed simulation.


This guide follows that journey. It covers the established Design Technology assessment structure used by November candidates completing the pre-2027 course. Because schools and examination sessions can be affected by curriculum transitions, confirm your level and assessment arrangements with your coordinator before relying on any timetable.


### Your three-week exam checklist


- Confirm whether you are entered for SL or HL.
- Learn the structure and duration of every paper you will sit.
- Practise interpreting command terms before writing answers.
- Allocate time in proportion to marks.
- Review weak topics through concise Study Notes and Flashcards.
- Complete targeted questions in the RevisionDojo Questionbank.
- Sit full timed papers in Exam mode.
- Review mistakes by cause, not merely by topic.


### Three weeks out: understand the papers


Imagine a Design Technology student opening a practice paper three weeks before the November session. The content looks familiar. The difficulty lies elsewhere: deciding how much to write, how to organise an evaluation and when to move on.


That is why paper structure matters. It turns an intimidating exam into a sequence of smaller decisions.


Assessment Level Duration Marks Weighting


Paper 1 SL 45 minutes 30 20%


Paper 2 SL 1 hour 30 minutes 50 40%


Paper 1 HL 1 hour 40 20%


Paper 2 HL 1 hour 30 minutes 50 20%


Paper 3 HL 1 hour 30 minutes 40 20%


Internal assessment SL and HL Completed in school Assessed through the design project 40%


Paper 1 consists of multiple-choice questions based on the core. Paper 2 combines data-based, short-answer and extended-response work. HL students also take Paper 3, which assesses the additional higher level material through structured questions.


These proportions reveal an important truth. SL students cannot treat Paper 2 as an afterthought because it carries twice the examination weighting of Paper 1. HL students face a more balanced written assessment, so a neglected paper creates a significant gap.


### Paper 1: make accuracy faster than doubt


Multiple-choice questions can feel simple because the answer is already on the page. In practice, the alternatives are designed to expose imprecise understanding.


Read the stem before studying the options. Identify whether it asks for the *best* , *most appropriate* , *least likely* or *primary* answer. A single qualifier can reverse the task.


Then predict the concept before looking closely at the choices. If the question concerns why a designer uses an anthropometric percentile, retrieve the principle first. This makes you less vulnerable to an option containing familiar but irrelevant terminology.


Use a three-pass method:


- **First pass:** answer questions you can solve confidently.
- **Second pass:** calculate, compare or eliminate options on harder questions.
- **Final pass:** revisit flagged items and check that every question has an answer.


For SL, 45 minutes across 30 marks gives an average of 1.5 minutes per mark. At HL, 60 minutes across 40 marks produces the same average. That is a guide, not a command. Some questions take seconds, leaving time for those involving close interpretation or calculation.


Do not repeatedly change an answer because it suddenly feels too obvious. Change it only when you can state the technical reason why another option is stronger.


### Paper 2: let the marks control the answer


Paper 2 rewards range. You may need to read data, recall terminology, explain a relationship and construct a sustained judgement within the same sitting.


A useful starting budget is about 1.8 minutes per mark because the paper offers 90 minutes for 50 marks. Reserve several minutes for checking, then adjust the remaining time across sections according to their marks.


### Data-based questions


Begin with the information provided, not a memorised paragraph. Read graph axes, units, labels, scales and table headings before drawing a conclusion.


If asked to calculate, show the substitution and include the unit. If asked to compare, refer to both values and quantify the difference where possible. If asked to suggest a reason, connect the observed pattern to a relevant design principle rather than merely restating the data.


A strong response often follows this sequence:


**Evidence from the stimulus + relevant concept + consequence for the product, user or manufacturer.**


### Short-answer questions


Marks are a practical guide to depth. A two-mark explanation usually needs more than two isolated facts. It commonly requires a valid point and a developed reason or consequence.


Consider the difference:


- Weak: “Injection moulding is fast.”
- Stronger: “Injection moulding has a short cycle time once tooling is established, allowing large quantities of identical polymer components to be produced efficiently.”


The second answer explains what “fast” means in a manufacturing context. It gives the examiner something specific to reward.


### Extended responses


Read every available option before committing. Choose the question that gives you the best combination of accurate knowledge, relevant examples and evaluative depth.


Plan briefly. A dependable structure is:


- define the issue in the context of the question;
- develop two or three distinct arguments;
- support them with design terminology and contextual examples;
- consider a limitation, trade-off or alternative;
- finish with a justified conclusion.


Evaluation is not a decorative sentence beginning with “however.” It is a judgement about competing priorities. A product may reduce material use but be difficult to repair. Automation may improve consistency but require high capital investment. The stronger answer explains which consideration matters most under the stated conditions.


A student presents an absurdly elaborate redesigned chair after being asked for one advantage


The joke is also an exam rule: answer the question that exists, not the more interesting question you wish had been asked.


### Paper 3: turn HL knowledge into connected reasoning


HL Paper 3 lasts 90 minutes and carries 40 marks. It tests additional higher level material through structured questions, so recall alone is rarely enough. The challenge is connecting technological knowledge with consequences for design decisions, systems and stakeholders.


Before writing, annotate the stimulus. Circle constraints, underline evidence and note the topic beside each relevant detail. This prevents generic answers that could apply to almost any product.


For a structured evaluation, use a chain of reasoning:


**Design decision → immediate effect → stakeholder or lifecycle consequence → qualified judgement.**


Suppose a question asks about choosing a sophisticated production process. Do not stop at accuracy. Consider tooling, production volume, labour, quality control, material waste, customisation and the point at which the investment becomes reasonable. HL marks often sit in these relationships.


Keep checking the command term. *Explain* requires reasons. *Discuss* requires a balanced consideration of issues. *Evaluate* requires a conclusion supported by criteria. *Suggest* allows a plausible response, but plausibility still needs to be grounded in the stimulus.


### Two weeks out: diagnose the reason for every lost mark


At two weeks, our hypothetical student stops saying, “I am bad at Topic 4.” That diagnosis is too broad to improve.


Instead, mistakes go into four categories:


Error type What it looks like Corrective action


Knowledge A term or process is unknown Review Study Notes and make a Flashcard


Interpretation Data or wording is misread Annotate units, qualifiers and context


Technique The response does not satisfy the command term Rewrite it using the mark allocation


Timing A complete answer is never attempted Practise under a fixed time limit


This is where RevisionDojo becomes more than a content library. Use the **Questionbank** to isolate a weak topic, then use **AI Chat** to clarify a concept without losing the context of the course. **Grading tools** can help you inspect whether a response contains enough development, while **Study Notes** and **Flashcards** repair the underlying knowledge efficiently.


Alternate focused practice with mixed sets. Topic-by-topic work builds competence, but mixed practice trains the harder skill of recognising which idea a question is testing.


### One week out: rehearse the real decision-making


The final week is not the moment to collect endless new resources. It is the moment to make familiar decisions under realistic pressure.


Sit timed practice in RevisionDojo **Exam mode** . Use Predicted Papers and Mock Exams to rehearse the complete experience: no notes, no pausing and no checking an answer halfway through. Afterwards, review every uncertain response, including correct guesses.


Build a final checklist from recurring errors. It might say:


- quote data with units;
- develop each explanation through cause and effect;
- apply answers to the named product;
- compare both sides explicitly;
- give a justified conclusion;
- move on when the time budget expires.


In the final 24 hours, favour retrieval over heavy rereading. Test definitions, manufacturing processes, material properties, innovation concepts and HL links from memory. Sleep and exam logistics are now part of technique because attention is one of the resources the paper measures indirectly.


### A calm November strategy


Good examination technique is disciplined selection. You select the relevant concept, the appropriate depth and the moment to stop. Three weeks of focused practice can make those choices feel less expensive.


Start with individual questions in the RevisionDojo **Questionbank** . Then sit timed papers in **Exam mode** , review them through the Grading tools and return to Study Notes only where the evidence says you should. With Flashcards, AI Chat, Predicted Papers, Mock Exams, the Coursework Library and Tutors available when deeper support is needed, RevisionDojo gives an IB Design Technology student one connected place to prepare.


The aim is not to enter the November session knowing every possible sentence. It is to recognise what each question deserves and deliver it before the clock moves on.
